title: The Tribunal at Nuremberg
subtitle: The International Military Tribunal, Nuremberg, 1945–1946
intro: On 20 November 1945, in a courtroom rebuilt inside Nuremberg's Palace of Justice, twenty-one leaders of the defeated German state sat in two rows of a wooden dock while judges from the United States, Britain, the Soviet Union and France heard the case against them. Nothing quite like it had been tried before: the victors had agreed in London on 8 August to put an enemy government on trial under a written charter, for planning aggressive war, for war crimes, and for a new category, crimes against humanity. The trial ran for almost a year. The judgment was read on 30 September and 1 October 1946; ten men were hanged in the prison gymnasium in the early hours of 16 October, and Hermann Göring escaped the rope by poison the evening before.

The court's own record is unusually full. Every word spoken was interpreted at once into four languages through headphones, taken down by stenographers and printed in the 42 volumes of the official 'Blue Series'. It is the main source here, and it carries the voices that no diary could: the defendants' pleas and testimony, the prosecutors' speeches, the cross-examinations, and witnesses ranging from an Auschwitz survivor, Marie-Claude Vaillant-Couturier, to the former Auschwitz commandant, Rudolf Höss. Atrocity evidence is reported here as the court recorded it, with figures and without detail.

Around the record stand the private and public writers. Thomas Dodd, the American trial counsel, wrote home to his wife every few days, and his letters give the trial's ordinary texture: staff quarrels, slow colleagues, homesickness, a week on the Riviera while the judges deliberated. David Maxwell Fyfe, who led the British in court, wrote to his wife too, though his letters are known here only through quotation. The prison psychologist G. M. Gilbert kept notes of his daily conversations with the defendants, published in 1947 as Nuremberg Diary: a real diary, but one written up for print by a man who made no secret of his views. Airey Neave, who served the indictment, set down his memories thirty years later.

The press supplied the rest. Janet Flanner's New Yorker 'Letters' of March 1946 judged that Göring had outplayed Jackson, and her editor sent Rebecca West to replace her; West's long reports caught the tedium of the court as sharply as the faces in the dock. Kingsbury Smith of the International News Service, chosen by lot, wrote the account of the executions that most of the world read. Some of these sources are dated diaries or letters, many are dated documents of the court, and some are reportage or later recollection; each is labelled for what it is.

Read together, they disagree. Dodd thought Jackson's cross-examination of Göring went well; Maxwell Fyfe and most reporters did not. Göring treated the trial as victors' justice; Speer accepted a general share of responsibility; Höss described his own work in figures. The judgment itself split: the Soviet judge dissented from the three acquittals. Where the court ruled, this chapter reports the ruling; it adds no verdict of its own on the questions the trial still raises about law made by victors.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian and in Central European Time as kept in Nuremberg. The executions took place after midnight and are dated 16 October 1946; Göring's death is dated 15 October. Where Dodd's and Maxwell Fyfe's letters are known only from extracts, their dates are as given in those extracts. Magazine pieces are dated by issue or dateline as stated.

eyes.name: International Military Tribunal (the court's own record)
eyes.role: Four judges and four alternates from the US, UK, USSR and France, presided over by Lord Justice Geoffrey Lawrence; its clerks, stenographers and interpreters produced the daily transcript in four languages
eyes.side: The four Allied powers acting under the London Charter
eyes.where: Courtroom 600, Palace of Justice, Nuremberg (first session in Berlin, 18 October 1945)
eyes.authenticity: The official text is the 42-volume 'Blue Series', Trial of the Major War Criminals before the International Military Tribunal (Nuremberg, 1947–49), volumes 2–22 being the proceedings. The English edition was checked against the recordings; the Avalon Project at Yale reproduces it day by day. Everything said in court passed through interpreters, and the printed text is a corrected version of the stenographers' notes.
eyes.bio: The record is the spine of this chapter: 218 days of sessions, about 240 witnesses heard in court and many thousands of documents. It preserves the defendants' own words under oath alongside those of the prosecutors and witnesses, which no diarist could do.

sources.title: Harvard Law School Nuremberg Trials Project (transcripts)

eyes.name: Robert H. Jackson
eyes.role: Associate Justice of the US Supreme Court, on leave as US Chief of Counsel for the Prosecution of Axis Criminality; aged 53
eyes.where: Washington and London in 1945, then the prosecution's table in Courtroom 600

waypoints.label: Washington, report to the President, June 1945

eyes.vantage_label: chief prosecutor and architect of the trial
eyes.form: speeches in court and official reports (US government publications)
eyes.authenticity: His opening and closing addresses are in the IMT record and were also printed by the US Government Printing Office in Nazi Conspiracy and Aggression (1946); his reports to President Truman were released by the State Department. As US-government texts they are quoted here in short phrases.
eyes.bio: Jackson had negotiated the London Charter and argued that aggressive war itself was a crime. His opening speech was the trial's high point; his cross-examination of Göring in March 1946 was widely judged a failure, a verdict his own staff recorded in letters.

sources.title: Robert H. Jackson Center: Jackson vs. Göring

eyes.name: Sir Hartley Shawcross
eyes.role: Attorney General in Attlee's Labour government and British Chief Prosecutor; aged 43; attended for the main speeches while his deputy ran the case day to day
eyes.where: Nuremberg for the opening and closing speeches; otherwise London
eyes.authenticity: Both speeches are in the IMT record (Blue Series vols 3 and 19). He kept no published trial diary; his later memoir Life Sentence (1995) is not used here.
eyes.bio: Shawcross built the British case on treaties broken and wars of aggression, and in his closing speech turned to the individual human cost, citing an eyewitness affidavit about a mass shooting in Ukraine. He spoke as a government minister as well as an advocate.

sources.title: UConn Human Rights Archives: Dodd letters on the British opening

eyes.name: Sir David Maxwell Fyfe
eyes.role: Conservative MP and former Attorney General; British Deputy Chief Prosecutor, the leader of the British team in court; aged 45
eyes.where: Nuremberg, living with the British delegation
eyes.authenticity: He wrote about 205 letters to his wife Sylvia between October 1945 and August 1946; they are in the Kilmuir Papers (Churchill Archives Centre, Cambridge) and are known here only through quotation in a 2025 Spectator article, so dates and wording are second-hand.
eyes.bio: Maxwell Fyfe followed Jackson in cross-examining Göring and was generally credited with doing better, by starting from the murder of fifty recaptured RAF officers after the 'Great Escape' from Stalag Luft III. Later, as Lord Kilmuir, he was Lord Chancellor; he wrote the foreword to the London edition of Gilbert's Nuremberg Diary.

sources.title: The Spectator: How Göring almost derailed the Nuremberg Trials (2025)

eyes.name: Roman Andreyevich Rudenko
eyes.role: Procurator of the Ukrainian SSR, Lieutenant-General of Justice and Soviet Chief Prosecutor; aged 38
eyes.where: Courtroom 600 and the Soviet delegation's quarters in Nuremberg
eyes.form: speeches and examinations in court (official record)
eyes.authenticity: His speeches survive in the IMT record (English text translated from the Russian) and in Soviet editions. No personal diary is known; the Soviet delegation's direction from Moscow, including a commission chaired by Andrei Vyshinsky, is documented in archives opened after 1991.
eyes.bio: Rudenko presented the case for the country that had suffered the greatest losses, and produced the trial's most dramatic surprise witness, Field Marshal Friedrich Paulus. The Soviet indictment also charged Germany with the Katyn massacre of Polish officers, a charge the judgment left out.

eyes.name: Thomas J. Dodd
eyes.role: Connecticut lawyer and former FBI agent and Justice Department prosecutor; interrogator, then US Executive Trial Counsel; aged 38
eyes.where: Nuremberg; Grand Hotel and the courtroom; a short leave in Cannes, September 1946
eyes.vantage_label: prosecutor writing home every few days
eyes.authenticity: Several hundred letters to his wife Grace, kept by the family; edited by his son Christopher J. Dodd with Lary Bloom as Letters from Nuremberg (Crown, 2007). The originals are at the University of Connecticut, whose archive blog published dated extracts in 2015–16. Modern publication: digested only.
eyes.bio: Dodd moved from interrogating prisoners to running the American case in court, presented the concentration-camp evidence and later the case against several defendants. His letters are candid about colleagues, the slow pace and his homesickness, and they give the trial's ordinary days.

sources.title: UConn Human Rights Archives: 70 Years After Nuremberg (Dodd letters)
Thomas Dodd and the Nuremberg Trials (Connecticut Explored)

eyes.name: Gustave Mark Gilbert
eyes.role: US Army captain and psychologist, fluent in German; prison psychologist with daily access to the defendants; aged 34
eyes.where: The cells and exercise yard of the Nuremberg jail; the courtroom, seated near the dock; the defendants' lunchroom
eyes.vantage_label: in the cells with the accused
eyes.authenticity: Nuremberg Diary (Farrar, Straus, 1947) is built from notes Gilbert says he wrote immediately after each conversation, but it was edited for publication and the defendants never checked it; some defence lawyers and later historians have questioned its fairness. The London edition (1948) omits one Göring remark. Digested only.
eyes.bio: Gilbert arrived on 20 October 1945, gave the defendants intelligence and Rorschach tests, and talked with them almost daily for a year. He also interviewed Rudolf Höss in April 1946. His diary is the nearest thing to the defendants' unguarded voices, filtered through a man openly hostile to what they had done.

sources.title: Göring's remark on war, from Nuremberg Diary (MIT page)

eyes.name: Airey Neave
eyes.role: British Army major, the first British officer to escape from Colditz; assigned to the Tribunal to serve the indictment and help the defendants find counsel; aged 29
eyes.authenticity: His certificate of service dated 24 October 1945 is in the IMT record (Blue Series vol. 1). His impressions of the defendants come from his book Nuremberg (1978), written thirty years on and excerpted in The Spectator in 1976; those are flagged as later recollection.
eyes.bio: Neave carried the indictment from cell to cell and watched each defendant receive it. A prisoner of the Germans only three years before, he later became a Conservative MP and was killed by an INLA bomb at Westminster in 1979.

sources.title: Certificate of service on individual defendants (Avalon)
The Spectator, 21 Feb 1976: 'The day of the indictment'

eyes.name: Marie-Claude Vaillant-Couturier
eyes.role: French photographer and journalist, Resistance member and Communist deputy in the Constituent Assembly; survivor of Auschwitz-Birkenau and Ravensbrück; aged 33
eyes.side: France; survivor witness for the French prosecution
eyes.authenticity: Her testimony and cross-examination are in the IMT record for 28 January 1946 (Blue Series vol. 6; English text translated from her French). USHMM holds film of her on the stand.
eyes.bio: She was the first woman to testify at the trial, and the only witness who had been an inmate of Auschwitz. She spoke as both survivor and reporter, insisting that she repeated only what she had seen or had checked with several others.

sources.title: USHMM film: Communist female prisoner testifies at Nuremberg Trial

eyes.name: Rudolf Höss
eyes.role: Former SS-Obersturmbannführer and commandant of Auschwitz (May 1940 – December 1943, and again in 1944); arrested by British troops in March 1946; aged 45
eyes.side: Germany (SS); witness called by the defence
eyes.where: Nuremberg jail and the witness stand
eyes.authenticity: Affidavit 3868-PS, signed at Nuremberg on 5 April 1946, and his testimony of 15 April 1946 are in the IMT record. He was not a defendant. His later autobiography, written in a Kraków prison before his trial and execution in Poland in 1947, is not used here.
eyes.bio: Called by Kaltenbrunner's counsel to show that Kaltenbrunner had no authority over the camps, Höss instead confirmed under oath the figures in his affidavit. His flat, administrative manner on the stand was remarked on by many in the courtroom.

eyes.name: Hermann Göring
eyes.role: Former Reichsmarschall, commander of the Luftwaffe and Hitler's designated successor; the senior surviving Nazi; aged 52
eyes.where: Front row of the dock, Courtroom 600; cell 5 of the Nuremberg jail
eyes.form: testimony and statements in court (official record)
eyes.authenticity: His plea, testimony (13–22 March 1946) and final statement are in the IMT record, translated by the court's interpreters. Remarks attributed to him outside court come from Gilbert's diary and others' memoirs and are labelled as such.
eyes.bio: Göring took the trial as a stage, led the other defendants in the dock and defended the regime rather than himself. He was convicted on all counts and sentenced to death, and killed himself in his cell about two hours before he was due to be hanged.

eyes.name: Albert Speer
eyes.role: Former architect to Hitler and Reich Minister of Armaments and War Production; defendant; aged 40
eyes.where: Second row of the dock; witness stand, June 1946
eyes.authenticity: His testimony (19–21 June 1946) and final statement (31 August 1946) are in the IMT record. His Spandau diaries and memoir were published in 1969–75 and reshaped his story; later research showed he knew more than he admitted. Not used here.
eyes.bio: Speer chose a strategy unlike any other defendant's: he accepted a general responsibility as a member of the leadership while denying knowledge of the extermination. He was convicted on war crimes and crimes against humanity for the use of forced labour and sentenced to twenty years.

eyes.name: Rebecca West
eyes.role: British novelist and critic reporting for The New Yorker and the Daily Telegraph; aged 53
eyes.where: Press seats and the press camp at Stein; visits in summer 1946 and for the judgment
eyes.authenticity: 'Extraordinary Exile' (New Yorker, 7 September 1946) and 'The Birch Leaves Falling' (dateline 19 October, published 26 October 1946), revised for A Train of Powder (1955). Copyright texts: digested only.
eyes.bio: West came to Nuremberg when Harold Ross replaced Janet Flanner, whose March 1946 'Letters' had judged Jackson outmatched by Göring. Her portraits of the defendants are some of the sharpest ever written, and she was candid about the boredom of the court.

sources.title: New Yorker, 'The Birch Leaves Falling' (NJ Holocaust curriculum reprint)

eyes.name: Joseph Kingsbury Smith
eyes.role: European general manager of the International News Service; chosen by lot as the American press witness at the executions; aged 38
eyes.where: The gymnasium of the Nuremberg jail, night of 15–16 October 1946
eyes.authenticity: His pool dispatch was distributed by INS on 16 October 1946 and printed in many papers that day. Copyright text: digested only, without its graphic detail.
eyes.bio: Eight journalists were admitted, two from each occupying power; Smith wrote the report most of the world read. He later became publisher of the New York Journal-American.

sources.title: Kingsbury Smith, 'The Execution of Nazi War Criminals' (Famous Trials)

entries.headline: Report to Truman: the case must rest on evidence, not vengeance
entries.digest: Jackson's report to the President, released by the White House, argued that the leaders should be tried rather than shot out of hand, and that the case should be built mainly from the regime's own captured documents. He proposed charging the waging of aggressive war as a crime in itself.
entries.source_note: Report to the President by Mr. Justice Jackson, June 6, 1945 (State Department Bulletin, 10 June 1945); release date as commonly cited.

entries.headline: Four powers sign the Charter that creates the court
entries.digest: The US, UK, USSR and France signed the London Agreement and its annexed Charter, setting up an International Military Tribunal of four judges. Article 6 defined crimes against peace, war crimes and crimes against humanity, and the Charter ruled out official position or superior orders as a complete defence.
entries.source_note: London Agreement and Charter, 8 Aug 1945 (Blue Series vol. 1).

entries.headline: The indictment is lodged in Berlin
entries.digest: At its only session in Berlin, with the Soviet judge Nikitchenko presiding, the Tribunal received the indictment against 24 individuals and six organisations on four counts: common plan or conspiracy, crimes against peace, war crimes, and crimes against humanity. The trial was set to open in Nuremberg.
entries.source_note: Blue Series vol. 1 (Berlin session).

entries.headline: Neave carries the indictment from cell to cell
entries.digest: Major Neave served each prisoner with a German copy of the indictment, the Charter and a list of German lawyers, and told each of his right to counsel. His certificate lists twenty men served at Nuremberg that day, Ley and Hess among them. In his much later book he remembered Göring as composed and contemptuous of the charges' legal basis, Hess as absorbed in a novel, and Ribbentrop as anxious about finding a lawyer.
entries.source_note: Certificate of service dated 24 Oct 1945 (Avalon v1-06); impressions from Neave, 'The day of the indictment', Spectator 21 Feb 1976 (memoir, written later).

entries.headline: A sudden promotion in the staff shake-up
entries.digest: Dodd told Grace it had been an unusual day: around six in the evening Colonel Storey showed him Jackson's order reorganising the American staff, placing Dodd among four men with full authority over the work. He was astonished.
entries.source_note: Letters from Nuremberg, 22 Oct 1945, via UConn blog 'A Rather Unusual Day' (28 Oct 2015).

entries.headline: The defendants write their verdicts on the indictment
entries.digest: Newly arrived, Gilbert asked each defendant to write a line on his copy of the indictment. Most wrote that they were personally innocent and blamed Hitler or Himmler, or dismissed the trial as victors' justice; Streicher and Rosenberg blamed the Jews. Robert Ley hanged himself in his cell that week, before the trial opened.
entries.source_note: Nuremberg Diary (1947), opening section; exact day of each comment not established here.

entries.headline: 'Not ready' three days before the opening
entries.digest: Dodd admitted that the prosecution was not ready for the 20 November start, and hoped they could improvise and still make a good showing. Two days earlier he had tested the new simultaneous-interpretation system, where a listener chose English, French, Russian or German with a dial.
entries.source_note: Letters from Nuremberg, 15 and 17 Nov 1945, via UConn blog 'At Long Last it Begins' (2 Dec 2015).

entries.headline: First day: twenty men in the dock, the indictment read aloud
entries.digest: Lord Justice Lawrence opened the trial. Of the 24 indicted, Ley was dead, Krupp was too ill to stand trial and Bormann was tried in his absence, so twenty-one sat in the dock. Prosecutors of the four nations took turns reading the indictment through the day.
entries.source_note: Blue Series vol. 2, first day.

entries.headline: Göring pleads, and is stopped from making a speech
entries.digest: Called first, Göring tried to read a statement before pleading and was told by the President that defendants could only plead. He then declared himself not guilty in the sense of the indictment; every other defendant followed with a not-guilty plea, some in their own phrasing.
entries.quote: I declare myself in the sense of the Indictment not guilty.
entries.source_note: Blue Series vol. 2, second day, pleas.

entries.headline: Jackson's opening: law in place of vengeance
entries.digest: Jackson spoke for most of the day. He said the crimes were so calculated and destructive that civilisation could not ignore them, and that the victors were choosing to try their enemies rather than punish them unheard. He promised to prove the case from the defendants' own documents and warned that the court would be judged by history.
entries.source_note: Opening statement, 21 Nov 1945 (Blue Series vol. 2; Nazi Conspiracy and Aggression vol. 1, GPO 1946).

entries.headline: The court watches film of the liberated camps
entries.digest: The American prosecution showed 'Nazi Concentration Camps', an hour of footage shot by Allied army cameramen as the camps were liberated. Lights were left on in the dock so the defendants' faces could be watched. The record notes the film's showing and its affidavits of authenticity; the court rose without further business.
entries.source_note: Blue Series vol. 2, 29 Nov 1945 (document 2430-PS).

entries.headline: Reactions in the dock and the cells
entries.digest: Gilbert and the psychiatrist Douglas Kelley watched the defendants during the film. He noted several men turning away or in tears and Schacht refusing to look; in the cells that evening some said they were ashamed, while Göring complained that the film had spoiled a good day in court for him.
entries.source_note: Nuremberg Diary (1947), entry for the film; wording of individual remarks is Gilbert's.

entries.headline: Lahousen testifies; Hess says his amnesia was a pretence
entries.digest: General Erwin Lahousen of the Abwehr, the first prosecution witness, described orders he had heard for operations in Poland and against Soviet prisoners. In the afternoon, during argument over his fitness to stand trial, Hess rose and announced that his memory had returned and that he had feigned its loss for tactical reasons. The Tribunal later ruled him fit.
entries.source_note: Blue Series vol. 2, 30 Nov 1945.

entries.headline: The British case: treaties broken, wars of aggression
entries.digest: Shawcross opened the British case on crimes against peace. He set out the treaties Germany had signed and broken and argued that by 1939 aggressive war was already outlawed, so the court was applying existing law rather than inventing it.
entries.source_note: Opening statement, 4 Dec 1945 (Blue Series vol. 3).

entries.headline: Praise for Shawcross, impatience with his own side
entries.digest: Dodd thought Shawcross had given a lawyer-like opening that was well received. He was less happy with his American colleague Sidney Alderman, who he felt dragged on for hours, and he hoped for a Christmas recess long enough to get home to Connecticut.
entries.source_note: Letters from Nuremberg, 6 Dec 1945, via UConn blog 'Presentation of the Cases' (9 Dec 2015).

entries.headline: Ohlendorf describes the mobile killing units
entries.digest: Otto Ohlendorf, who had led Einsatzgruppe D from June 1941 to June 1942, was examined by Colonel John Harlan Amen. He testified calmly that his units had reported about 90,000 people killed in that year, including women and children, and that the orders had come orally before the invasion of the Soviet Union.
entries.source_note: Avalon 01-03-46 (26th day).

entries.headline: France opens: de Menthon on crimes against the human person
entries.digest: The French chief prosecutor François de Menthon, a former Resistance leader, opened the French case, describing Nazism as an attack on the very idea of the human person and setting out the occupation of western Europe, forced labour and deportations.
entries.source_note: Blue Series vol. 5, 17 Jan 1946.

entries.headline: A survivor of Auschwitz takes the stand
entries.digest: Examined by the French prosecutor Charles Dubost, Vaillant-Couturier described her arrest in 1942, her deportation in January 1943 in a convoy of about 230 French women of whom 49 returned, and her time in Birkenau and Ravensbrück. Cross-examined for the SS by Dr Hans Marx about how she had survived and what Germans could have known, she answered that she had repeated only what she had seen or checked with several witnesses.
entries.quote: I have never quoted anything which has not previously been verified
entries.source_note: Avalon 01-28-46 (44th day).

entries.headline: The Soviet case opens
entries.digest: Rudenko opened for the USSR, describing the invasion of 22 June 1941 as premeditated aggression and setting out the destruction in the occupied Soviet territories, the treatment of prisoners of war and the killing of civilians.
entries.source_note: Blue Series vol. 7, 8 Feb 1946.

entries.headline: A surprise witness: Field Marshal Paulus
entries.digest: Rudenko's team produced Friedrich Paulus, who had surrendered at Stalingrad and been held in Soviet captivity. Paulus testified that the attack on the USSR had been planned well in advance, naming Keitel and Jodl among those responsible; the defendants, who had not known he was in Nuremberg, were visibly shaken.
entries.source_note: Blue Series vol. 7, 11–12 Feb 1946.

entries.headline: Göring begins his own defence
entries.digest: Questioned by his counsel Otto Stahmer, Göring gave a long, fluent account of his career and the regime, defending the seizure of power, rearmament and the Four-Year Plan, and claiming credit rather than denying it. His testimony ran over several days and impressed even hostile observers with its command of detail.
entries.source_note: Blue Series vol. 9, from 13 Mar 1946.

entries.headline: Jackson cross-examines Göring
entries.digest: Jackson's cross-examination began on the afternoon of 18 March and ran to 20 March. He lost several early exchanges over documents and translations and protested to the bench that Göring was making speeches instead of answering; on 20 March he took Göring through the anti-Jewish decrees from 1935 to 1941, the November 1938 pogrom and the seizure of art.
entries.source_note: Avalon 03-20-46 (86th day); Robert H. Jackson Center.

entries.headline: Jackson 'in good form' against a tired Göring
entries.digest: Dodd wrote that Jackson's cross-examination had taken the whole day, that Jackson had done well, and that Göring looked ill. His letter is a loyal counterweight to the press verdict that Jackson had been beaten.
entries.source_note: Letters from Nuremberg, p. 267, via UConn blog 'Göring on the stand' (23 Mar 2016).

entries.headline: Göring is 'extremely clever', but knocked off his perch
entries.digest: Maxwell Fyfe told his wife that Göring had been very clever, calm and factual, though a little dull, and that his own cross-examination, built on the shooting of the fifty RAF officers recaptured after the Stalag Luft III escape, had gone off all right and knocked Göring reasonably off his perch.
entries.source_note: Letter to Sylvia Maxwell Fyfe, quoted in The Spectator (2025); Kilmuir Papers.

entries.headline: 'At last finished with Göring'
entries.digest: He wrote that they had at last finished with Göring, after Soviet and French cross-examination, and that Hess's case would follow on the Monday.
entries.source_note: Letter quoted in The Spectator (2025).

entries.headline: Grumbling at Amen and at Judge Biddle
entries.digest: Dodd complained that Colonel Amen had wasted two hours on repetitive questions to win publicity, and that the American judge Francis Biddle had done more than anyone to slow the trial, his remarks taking up the rest of the day.
entries.source_note: Letters from Nuremberg, pp. 271–272, via UConn blog.

entries.headline: Höss signs an affidavit
entries.digest: In an affidavit taken in Nuremberg, Höss set out his service as commandant of Auschwitz and gave his estimate of the number of people killed there, about three million in all including those who died of hunger and disease. Later scholarship puts the number killed at Auschwitz at about 1.1 million; Höss's figures were his own.
entries.source_note: Document 3868-PS (USA-819), per Avalon 04-15-46.

entries.headline: Gilbert interviews the former commandant
entries.digest: Gilbert spoke with Höss in his cell several times. He recorded a man who described mass killing as a technical assignment, said he had never questioned Himmler's orders, and showed no emotion; Gilbert used the word apathetic to sum him up.
entries.source_note: Nuremberg Diary (1947), April 1946 entries on Höss; exact days not checked here.

entries.headline: Called for the defence, Höss confirms the affidavit
entries.digest: Höss was called by Kaltenbrunner's counsel, Dr Kurt Kauffmann, to show that Kaltenbrunner had no authority over the camps. Instead, examined and then cross-examined by Colonel Amen, he confirmed his affidavit, testified that he had commanded Auschwitz from May 1940 to December 1943, and said that Himmler had told him in 1941 of Hitler's order and demanded strict secrecy.
entries.quote: the Fuehrer had given the order for a final solution
entries.source_note: Avalon 04-15-46 (108th day).

entries.headline: Göring on how nations are led to war
entries.digest: Sweating in his cell, Göring told Gilbert that ordinary people never want war, but that leaders can always bring them along, whatever the system, by telling them they are under attack and condemning pacifists as unpatriotic. Gilbert objected that in a democracy the people have a say through their representatives; Göring was unmoved.
entries.source_note: Nuremberg Diary (1947), 18 Apr 1946; the remark is omitted from the 1948 London edition.

entries.headline: Speer accepts a share of the leadership's responsibility
entries.digest: Examined by his counsel Hans Flächsner, Speer described his work as armaments minister and his use of forced labour, and said that a leader must bear responsibility for the regime's catastrophe as a whole, even for what he did not know. He also described his opposition to Hitler's scorched-earth orders in 1945.
entries.source_note: Blue Series vol. 16, 19–20 Jun 1946.

entries.headline: Jackson cross-examines Speer
entries.digest: Jackson pressed Speer on the forced-labour programme and conditions in the armaments factories, but the exchange was courteous compared with the Göring cross-examination; Speer kept to his line of general responsibility without personal knowledge of the killings.
entries.source_note: Blue Series vol. 16, 21 Jun 1946.

entries.headline: Drafting the Justice's final speech; the defendants look doomed
entries.digest: Dodd apologised for not writing: he had been working hard on Jackson's closing speech while the defence lawyers delivered their final arguments. He noticed that the defendants seemed to sense the end coming: Göring was grey and dejected, and Keitel already wore what he called the mask of the doomed.
entries.source_note: Letters from Nuremberg, pp. 335–336, via UConn blog 'Mask of the doomed' (20 Jul 2016).

entries.headline: Jackson's closing: no innocence without denying the war
entries.digest: In his summation Jackson took each defendant's claim of ignorance in turn and set it against the documents. He ended by saying that a verdict of not guilty would be as true as saying there had been no war, no dead and no crime.
entries.quote: as true to say that there has been no war
entries.source_note: Closing address, 26 Jul 1946 (Blue Series vol. 19).

entries.headline: Shawcross's closing: the individual behind the numbers
entries.digest: Shawcross argued that each defendant shared in the murders as a member of the leadership. To make the scale concrete he read from the affidavit of the German engineer Hermann Gräbe about a mass shooting near Dubno in Ukraine, which he had witnessed in 1942, and asked the court to see the victims as people rather than statistics.
entries.source_note: Closing speech (Blue Series vol. 19, 26–27 Jul 1946).

entries.headline: Final statement: a denial to the end
entries.digest: In the defendants' final statements Göring denied that he had ordered or known of the mass killings, condemned them, and said he had never wanted war; he called the trial the victors' judgment and said the German people should not be blamed.
entries.source_note: Blue Series vol. 22, 31 Aug 1946.

entries.headline: Speer's final statement: a warning about technology
entries.digest: Speer spoke of the regime as the first dictatorship to use modern technology to dominate its people, and warned that a future war fought with atomic weapons could destroy civilisation. The court then adjourned to consider its judgment for a month.
entries.source_note: Blue Series vol. 22, 31 Aug 1946.

entries.headline: 'Extraordinary Exile': a court sunk in tedium
entries.digest: West described a courtroom where everyone, from the judges to the guards, was weary after ten months, and a town of ruins around it. She drew pitiless sketches of the defendants, including Göring as soft and theatrical, and of the occupation community marooned in Nuremberg.
entries.source_note: The New Yorker, 7 Sep 1946; later in A Train of Powder (1955).

entries.headline: On leave on the Riviera as the verdict is delayed
entries.digest: Writing from Cannes, Dodd described the beaches, Nice and the Monte Carlo casino, then reported that the judgment had been postponed a week; he was disappointed, given how long the trial had already run.
entries.source_note: Letters from Nuremberg, 19 Sep 1946, via UConn blog 'The end draws near' (28 Sep 2016).

entries.headline: His last full letter from Germany
entries.digest: Back in Nuremberg, Dodd called this his last full letter: the verdict was expected the coming Monday and Tuesday, Jackson had thanked him warmly for his work, and he planned to leave as soon as the sentences were read and sail home from Bremerhaven.
entries.source_note: Letters from Nuremberg, 26 Sep 1946, via UConn blog.

entries.headline: The judgment is read: law, organisations, the conspiracy
entries.digest: The judges took turns reading the judgment. It held that aggressive war was the supreme international crime, found the SS, SD, Gestapo and the Nazi Leadership Corps to be criminal organisations, but declined to so declare the SA, the Reich Cabinet and the General Staff and High Command. It narrowed the conspiracy count to planning aggressive war.
entries.source_note: Judgment, 30 Sep – 1 Oct 1946 (Blue Series vol. 1 and 22).

entries.headline: Verdicts and sentences; the Soviet judge dissents
entries.digest: Nineteen defendants were convicted and three, Schacht, von Papen and Fritzsche, acquitted. In the afternoon each convicted man was brought up alone to hear his sentence: twelve to death by hanging (Bormann in his absence), three to life imprisonment, four to terms of ten to twenty years. The Soviet judge Iona Nikitchenko filed a dissent against the acquittals, Hess's life sentence and the failure to condemn the Reich Cabinet and General Staff.
entries.source_note: Blue Series vol. 22, 1 Oct 1946.

entries.headline: Twenty years
entries.digest: Speer, convicted on counts three and four for the forced-labour programme, was sentenced to twenty years. The judgment noted in mitigation that he had opposed Hitler's destruction orders at the end of the war. He served the full term in Spandau.
entries.source_note: Blue Series vol. 22, 1 Oct 1946.

entries.headline: Visiting each man after his sentence
entries.digest: Gilbert went down the cell block as the men returned from the courtroom. He recorded Göring pale and asking to be left alone after saying the single word of his sentence, Speer saying twenty years was fair enough, and Fritzsche, acquitted, scarcely believing it.
entries.source_note: Nuremberg Diary (1947), final entries.

entries.headline: The last two days in court
entries.digest: West was in the press gallery for the judgment. She recorded the long reading, the ban on photographing the men as they heard their sentences, and the strangeness of the condemned walking out one by one through the sliding door at the back of the dock.
entries.source_note: 'The Birch Leaves Falling', New Yorker 26 Oct 1946 (NJ curriculum reprint).

entries.headline: Final report to the President
entries.digest: Jackson's final report to Truman claimed the trial had made aggressive war a crime under international law and had documented the regime's record from its own files, for the use of historians. He had resigned his post as chief of counsel and returned to the Supreme Court.
entries.source_note: Report to the President, 7 Oct 1946 (US State Dept., Report of Robert H. Jackson, 1949).

entries.headline: Göring takes poison before the hangings
entries.digest: Late in the evening, about two hours before he was due to be hanged, Göring killed himself with a cyanide capsule he had kept hidden. He left several letters; he had earlier asked in vain to be shot rather than hanged. How he had kept the poison hidden was never settled.
entries.source_note: Kingsbury Smith INS report, 16 Oct 1946 (timing); details of the letters from later accounts.

entries.headline: Ten men hanged before dawn
entries.digest: Smith reported that the ten condemned men were hanged one after another on gallows built in the prison gymnasium, beginning with Ribbentrop shortly after 1 a.m. and ending with Seyss-Inquart at about 2.45 a.m., before some thirty witnesses including eight correspondents. Göring's body was then brought in and shown to the witnesses.
entries.source_note: INS pool report, 16 Oct 1946 (Famous Trials reprint).

entries.headline: 'The Birch Leaves Falling': the news of Göring
entries.digest: West wrote of hearing about Göring's suicide and how it unsettled her sense of what the year-long trial had meant, and of the ruined statues and streets of Berlin seen on the journey. She set the condemned men beside William Joyce, hanged in London that January for treason, whose trial she had also reported.
entries.source_note: New Yorker, published 26 Oct 1946 (NJ curriculum reprint).

convergences.label: The indictment reaches the cells
convergences.note: The court's certificate records only names, dates and places; Neave's later memoir supplies faces and first reactions; Gilbert, arriving the next day, collected the defendants' written comments on the same document; Dodd, the same week, was promoted to run the case it set out.

convergences.label: Pleas and the opening speech
convergences.note: Göring tried to turn his plea into a speech and was stopped; Jackson was allowed most of a day. The transcript keeps both, the defendant's words and the prosecutor's, in the same record.

convergences.label: The camp film and Hess's announcement
convergences.note: The record notes only that a film was shown and authenticated; Gilbert, watching the dock, wrote down who looked away. The next afternoon the transcript caught Hess's own surprise statement.

convergences.label: The French case and its witnesses
convergences.note: De Menthon's opening framed the occupation in terms of principle; eleven days later a survivor supplied first-hand testimony, and a defence lawyer tested how she could know what she claimed.

convergences.label: Göring under cross-examination
convergences.note: The transcript shows Jackson struggling; his own deputy Dodd wrote home that he did well; the British deputy, who followed, privately judged Göring very clever and his own approach more effective. The press largely agreed with the British.

convergences.label: Höss in April
convergences.note: Höss's sworn figures entered the record through a defence witness meant to help Kaltenbrunner; in the same week Gilbert interviewed him in his cell and, on 18 April, heard Göring explain how peoples are led to war.

convergences.label: The closing speeches
convergences.note: Dodd's letter of 16 July shows the closing speech being drafted behind the scenes; Jackson's version answered the defendants' claims of ignorance with documents, while Shawcross, the next day, chose a single eyewitness account.

convergences.label: Judgment and sentence
convergences.note: The court's sentences, the convicted men's reactions in the cells, a novelist's view from the press gallery and a prosecutor counting the days until he could sail home all fall on the same two days.

convergences.label: The night of the executions
convergences.note: Göring's suicide on the evening of 15 October overshadowed the sentence carried out hours later; Smith's wire report gave the world the facts, and West, days later, wondered what Göring's escape from the gallows had done to the meaning of the trial.

ties.note: Jackson cross-examined Göring from 18 to 20 March 1946; the exchange is usually counted Göring's best days in court.
Dodd was Jackson's Executive Trial Counsel and, by his own letters, worked on drafting Jackson's closing speech; Jackson thanked him before leaving.
Maxwell Fyfe followed Jackson in cross-examining Göring and pinned him on the murder of the Stalag Luft III escapers.
Shawcross was British Chief Prosecutor; Maxwell Fyfe, his deputy and political opponent at home, led the British team in court day by day.
Neave served Göring with the indictment on 19 October 1945 and recorded his reaction in his memoir.
Gilbert talked with Göring in his cell through the year, including the conversation of 18 April 1946 most often quoted from his diary.
Gilbert interviewed Höss in the Nuremberg jail in April 1946, around the time of his testimony.
Maxwell Fyfe wrote the foreword to the London edition of Gilbert's Nuremberg Diary (1948).
Vaillant-Couturier was a prisoner in Birkenau from January 1943 to 1944, while Höss commanded the Auschwitz complex; both described the camp to the same court, eleven weeks apart.
Jackson cross-examined Speer on 21 June 1946, far more gently than he had Göring.
Allies in the prosecution, they differed on the Soviet Katyn charge, which the Tribunal heard in July 1946 and the judgment left out.
West's New Yorker portraits of Göring in the dock were among the most widely read descriptions of him.
Smith's execution report opened with Göring's suicide and recorded his body being shown to the witnesses.

threads_out.note: The trial judged the leaders of the war whose diaries fill the Volume I chapter: the invasions of Poland and the Soviet Union, the occupation of western Europe and the camps were all presented in Courtroom 600, largely from captured German records.

At Yalta in February 1945 the Big Three agreed only that the question of the major war criminals would go to their foreign ministers; Churchill had earlier favoured summary execution, and it was the US proposal for a trial that the London Conference turned into the Charter of 8 August 1945.

The Charter of the International Military Tribunal for the Far East, issued in January 1946, copied Nuremberg's categories of crime, and the Tokyo trial opened in May 1946 while Nuremberg was still sitting.

The Versailles Treaty had called for the Kaiser to be tried for 'a supreme offence against international morality', a trial that never happened; Nuremberg's prosecutors cited that failure and the weak Leipzig trials of 1921 as reasons to do it properly this time.

Andrei Vyshinsky, chief prosecutor of the Moscow show trials, chaired the Soviet commission that directed the Soviet team at Nuremberg and visited the city during the trial; Rudenko later prosecuted the U-2 pilot Gary Powers in Moscow in 1960.
